domain: Autonomy, robotics, ISRU, life support and human spaceflight systems

bottlenecks.name: Verifying autonomous behavior (planners, fault responses, learned perception, multi-robot teams)
bottlenecks.description: Showing that a rover, excavator, assembly robot or habitat fault manager does the right thing across the situations it will meet, when ground control is 1.3 s (Moon) to 4-24 min (Mars) away or blacked out behind a crater rim. Today the main method is human plan review plus simulation: Perseverance's first AI-planned drives (Dec 8 and 10, 2025; 210 m and 246 m, planned with Anthropic's Claude) were checked by running the commands through JPL's digital twin across more than 500,000 telemetry variables before uplink. CADRE (three cooperating rovers, launching on IM-3, planned late 2026) will be NASA's first multi-robot autonomous team beyond Earth, without formal proofs of its leader election or task re-allocation.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~25% of the domain's mathematical and modeling effort (judgment, general); the largest recurring cost in operating surface robots
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly 'solved in principle but expensive and expert-scarce': reactive synthesis from temporal-logic specs, probabilistic model checking, reachability and barrier certificates, runtime-assurance (Simplex) proofs all exist but each application needs a specialist to build abstractions and specs. On-demand research math collapses that cost (P1->P2). Genuinely open: verifying learned perception and large neural controllers at scale (closed-loop neural verification still does not scale to autonomy-size networks, arXiv 2609.16298, Sep 2026). Catalog touch: family 104 (mean-payoff/stochastic/parity games, T3) and the hardness family for planning ceilings; both small.

bottlenecks.name: Regolith and contact physics (granular flow, terramechanics, frictional contact, sintering)
bottlenecks.description: Every excavator, conveyor, wheel, drill, grasp, connector mate and sintered landing pad depends on models of granular media and frictional contact that are not predictive. Polar icy regolith is the worst case: lab tests (Sep 2026) show excavation energy for ice-cemented simulant rising from 2.74 to 143 J/g as ice goes from 1 to 12 wt% (52x), while pressure-sintered ice gets easier to dig with more ice; nobody knows which form exists at the poles. Granular continuum models (e.g. mu(I) rheology) are ill-posed in parts of their range (general), so codes regularize ad hoc; DEM is accurate but expensive. Contact simulators (MuJoCo, Drake, PhysX) use different contact regularizations and disagree in stick-slip and jamming (general).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Two genuinely open math problems with leverage: well-posedness/selection for frictional multi-contact dynamics and convergence of the time-stepping schemes used in simulators; and well-posed continuum theories of dense granular flow. AI can attack both (P1->P5->P6). But the dominant uncertainty is data (regolith ice form, dusty-vacuum friction and adhesion), which only landed missions and low-gravity experiments provide. No catalog family addresses these directly.

bottlenecks.name: ISRU process development and scale-up (oxygen from regolith, water ice, Mars CO2 to propellant)
bottlenecks.description: High-temperature multiphysics (molten-oxide electrochemistry at ~1,600 C, carbothermal reduction, solid-oxide CO2 electrolysis, Sabatier), electrode and crucible life, regolith handling and thermal management, scaled from lab rates to plant rates. Demonstrated: MOXIE peaked at 12 g O2/h on Mars (122 g total, 2021-23); KSC/Lunar Resources LR-1 molten regolith electrolysis produced 0.07 kg O2/h for 9 h from 25 kg of simulant in vacuum (late 2024); NASA/Sierra Space CaRD integrated solar-carbothermal prototype confirmed CO production (Feb 2026); Blue Origin's Air Pioneer MRE reactor extracted oxygen (Jun 2026); OxEon MOMS targets 1-3 kg O2/h plus methane. Targets: ~10 t O2/yr (~1.1 kg/h) at under 30 kW for a lunar plant; ~25 t O2 for a NASA-style Mars ascent vehicle; roughly 1,000 t of methalox per Starship return (general).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mostly expert-scarce, not open: reduced-order multiphysics models with error bounds, model-predictive control, Bayesian optimal experimental design to cut test count. The binding gates are physical: anode and crucible life (endurance tests run 10^3-10^4 hours), test-facility throughput (thermal-vacuum chambers that tolerate molten regolith), surface power, and landing opportunities. AI compresses design iterations, perhaps by 1-2 years in S2, but not endurance or launch.

bottlenecks.name: Life-support reliability and loop closure (physico-chemical and bioregenerative)
bottlenecks.description: Sizing spares and crew maintenance for regenerative ECLSS, raising oxygen and water recovery, and stabilizing bioregenerative loops (microbes, algae, plants, crew). ISS reached 98% water recovery (Brine Processor, Jun 2023), but the last public ECLSS reliability dataset dates from 2004 (ICES 2025). A 2025 Bayesian analysis from ISS data estimates 907 crew-hours of ECLSS maintenance (~45 min/day) and availability 0.9687 for a 1,200-day Mars mission, with the 5th-percentile spares mass equivalent to a 10x MTBF improvement, so uncertainty spans an order of magnitude. MELiSSA's pilot plant has integrated up to four compartments (2025). Artemis II (Apr 1-11, 2026) still had a urine vent line freeze.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Reliability and sparing math is solved in principle (semi-Markov, Bayesian) but hard to scale to system-of-systems, so expert time is the unlock (P1). Bioregenerative stability theory is partly open; family 149 (permanence for weakly reversible mass-action networks, T1) is an idealized building block. Binding: operating hours (a zero-failure demonstration at 95% confidence needs about 3x the target MTBF in unit-hours, general) and long closed-loop tests.

bottlenecks.name: Crew health and radiation risk
bottlenecks.description: Estimating cancer, cardiovascular and CNS risk from galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events, and providing Earth-independent medical care. NASA's career limit is 600 mSv effective dose; a 2026 Space Weather study finds Mars missions on minimum-energy trajectories stay below 1,000 mSv in active solar cycles but stay below 600 mSv only near solar maximum or on faster transfers. Dose transport is well validated (blind Artemis I comparisons, 2025); biological risk per unit dose is not (high-LET radiobiology, dose-rate effects, transfer from terrestrial epidemiology).
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Small. Transport and dosimetry math is mature. Risk-model uncertainty is data-bound: no human high-LET cohort exists and animal cancer studies take years per cohort. AI helps assemble mechanistic models and medical decision support (P1), not the biology.

bottlenecks.name: Operations planning and logistics under delay (scheduling, task allocation, comm windows, power)
bottlenecks.description: Scheduling dozens of robots and crew tasks around two-week lunar nights, crater-rim comm blackouts, battery limits and launch cadence; NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 2026) targets up to 30 robotic landings from 2027 and crewed landings every six months, which multiplies the number of assets per operator.
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Largely expert-scarce custom planning and optimization (P1). The catalog's hardness results (102 UGC, 125 k-median 1+2/e, T3; 124 three-machine scheduling, 110 k-server, 111 prophet inequalities, T1) set ceilings (P3) but rarely bind on small, structured real instances.

nodes.title: Reaction networks that never lose a species
nodes.description: Family 149 claims the permanence (boundedness plus persistence) conjecture for every finite weakly reversible mass-action reaction network: all concentrations stay between epsilon and 1/epsilon forever, whatever the positive rate constants. Once independently confirmed it becomes a theorem-level guarantee for idealized closed chemical and microbial loop models.
nodes.status_oct2026: Family 149, T1 per the release overview and the analyst catalog (no entry in lean/formalization.yaml). Newer detail found in the repo: lean/docs/149.md describes a Lean formalization of global boundedness and persistence with a Comparator statement (ComparatorChallenges/MassAction.lean). If that holds up it would be T3 for the formal part. No outside Comparator run reported as of 2026-10-07; repo has a single commit (Oct 6).
nodes.why: Persistence and permanence of weakly reversible networks sit at the core of chemical reaction network theory (the global attractor conjecture family, open for decades, general). 'Achieved' here means independently checked (Comparator run plus statement audit) or reconstructed by CRN theorists. Because a formal statement already exists, verification is a checking task, not a research task; under S2/S3 checking bandwidth is abundant. Under S1 the field is niche and may not be prioritized by volunteer checkers, hence Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Real life-support loops are not closed weakly reversible mass-action systems: they include harvesting, control inputs, light-limited and saturating kinetics (Monod, Michaelis-Menten), growth and death, contamination and small-population noise. The epsilon in the theorem depends on network, rates and initial state and may be numerically useless. The result raises confidence in a modeling idealization, not in any habitat.
nodes.signpost: An independent Comparator run on MassAction.lean posted to Hexagon or by a recognized checker (Buzzard, Tao, Mathlib maintainers), plus reuse by CRN theorists within 12 months.

nodes.title: Rigorous theory of frictional contact
nodes.description: Existence, uniqueness or explicit selection rules for rigid and near-rigid bodies with many frictional contacts and impacts (the Painleve paradox regime), plus convergence proofs and rates for the time-stepping schemes that robot simulators actually use. This is the mathematics under every grasp, docking latch, connector mate, wheel-soil contact and assembly simulation.
nodes.status_oct2026: Open (general). Rigid-body Coulomb friction can admit no solution or many; measure-differential-inclusion time-stepping schemes (Stewart-Trinkle, Anitescu-Potra) converge only in weak senses and without practical rates. No catalog family addresses it. The pattern is the same as family 363 (Boltzmann nonuniqueness): an equation that does not by itself pin down the physics, so a selection principle is needed.
nodes.why: Outside teams can pose this only once research-grade math is purchasable (S2: 2027). It is a hard but well-specified applied-analysis problem of the kind the release shows the capability can now reach (cf. the forced Navier-Stokes blowup claim of Sep 2026 and the PDE families). Under S2's 6-9 month doubling of solvable depth, a convergence theorem for at least one widely used regularization with computable rates is plausible by 2028. A negative result (nonuniqueness in configurations robots actually hit) would be equally useful: it tells simulator developers where results are artifacts of the chosen regularization.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Practitioners already get usable results from compliant contact tuned to test data; the residual sim-to-real gap in grasping and assembly is dominated by unknown parameters (friction coefficients, dust adhesion, cable stiffness), which a theorem about idealized Coulomb friction does not touch.
nodes.signpost: An AI-produced paper resolving a named contact-mechanics question (convergence with rates for a mainstream time-stepping scheme, or classification of Painleve non-uniqueness) accepted in an applied-math or mechanics venue, or formalized in Lean, by end-2028.

nodes.title: Well-posed equations for flowing regolith
nodes.description: Prove well-posedness (or pinpoint ill-posedness and its minimal regularization) for continuum models of dense granular flow such as mu(I) rheology and nonlocal granular-fluidity models, so excavation, conveying, berm-building and plume-cratering codes converge under mesh refinement for physical reasons rather than tuned numerics.
nodes.status_oct2026: Open (general). mu(I) rheology is known to be ill-posed at low and high inertial numbers (Barker et al., J. Fluid Mech. 2015, general); nonlocal models exist without a global well-posedness theory. No catalog family addresses granular media.
nodes.why: Regolith handling is simulated today with DEM (10^6-10^8 particles, days to weeks per design point, general) or with continuum/MPM codes built on rheologies that are not well-posed. A proven-convergent continuum model would make design sweeps 100-1,000x cheaper than DEM (general estimate) and trustworthy under refinement, feeding excavation and sintering design. Under S2 this is an AI-applied-math problem of 2028-29 difficulty; S3 a year earlier.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Engineers already regularize empirically and DEM is adequate for bucket-scale design. The 52x spread in excavation energy across plausible polar ice forms dwarfs any modeling error a theorem removes.
nodes.signpost: An AI-produced well-posedness or ill-posedness theorem for a named granular rheology, then adoption of the selected model in an open-source MPM or continuum granular code.

nodes.title: Correct-by-construction mission planners
nodes.description: Planners, schedulers and fault responses generated automatically from temporal-logic specifications (reactive synthesis, energy/mean-payoff games, probabilistic model checking) at the scale of real surface operations, each shipped with a proof that the plan meets the spec under the modeled environment.
nodes.status_oct2026: Theory mature, flight use rare: synthesis works for small specs, but abstractions (terrain, energy, comm windows) and specs are built by scarce experts (general). Family 104 (T3, Lean in repo, unchecked) gives quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff and turn-based stochastic games; the formalized part is a randomized quasipolynomial algorithm for mean-payoff games. Mean-payoff ('energy') objectives match battery-constrained rovers.
nodes.why: The cost of synthesis is building a sound abstraction and a correct spec, which is exactly bespoke expert math. An agent that proposes the abstraction, proves it sound, writes the spec, synthesizes the controller and emits Lean or model-checker certificates turns months of formal-methods work into days. 'Achieved' = a synthesized planner for a realistic multi-day surface scenario (energy, thermal, comm windows, faults) with machine-checked certificate, produced with under 10% specialist effort. Family 104 changes the theoretical ceiling for stochastic and mean-payoff games, but practical solvers (Zielonka, strategy iteration) already handle realistic sizes, so its own contribution is P3, small.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Mission operations culture values human-readable, human-reviewed plans; even the AI-planned Perseverance drives were validated by simulation, not proof. Specs, not proofs, are the hard part, and a proof of the wrong property adds little (analyst position h).
nodes.signpost: A CLPS, LTV or NASA surface payload announces spec-to-plan synthesized autonomy in flight software, or ESA/NASA solicitations require correct-by-construction planners.

nodes.title: Known limits for robot fleet scheduling
nodes.description: Hardness and optimality results tell surface-ops planners which multi-robot task-allocation, scheduling, partitioning and depot-siting problems can be solved near-optimally and which cannot, so effort moves to problem structure, exact solvers on small instances and heuristics.
nodes.status_oct2026: 102 Unique Games Conjecture (T3) fixes optimal approximation ratios for many labeling and partitioning problems; 125 metric k-median threshold 1+2/e (T3) bounds depot, charging-pad and relay siting; 124 polynomial-time unit-job scheduling on three identical machines with precedence (T1 per release overview; repo lean/docs/124.md lists a Comparator statement, so possibly T3); 110 optimal randomized k-server (T1) and 111 one-sample matroid prophet inequalities (T1; competitive ratio 2^-310, no polynomial-time implementation asserted) for online dispatch.
nodes.premise_tier: T3 (102, 125); T1 (124, 110, 111): conditional for those parts
nodes.why: A lunar base with dozens of robots and crew visits every six months is an online scheduling and allocation problem with precedence constraints. Ceilings act in months: they stop teams chasing general-purpose 'optimal' fleet planners and let them judge vendor claims. 124 is a cute fit for a three-robot team with precedence-constrained unit tasks. The parts resting on 124, 110 and 111 are conditional (T1).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Real instances are small and structured and are solved well by MILP/CP solvers; worst-case hardness and galactic constants (111's 2^-310) say little about them. Most of these results were already believed; the change is from belief to theorem.
nodes.signpost: Planning papers or vendor documentation for lunar and Mars operations cite these ceilings when scoping fleet planners; otherwise no measurable change expected.

nodes.title: Contact simulators with error bars
nodes.description: Physics engines for grasping, latching, digging and assembly that carry proven convergence and computable error bounds for stated friction and compliance parameters, so a simulation run can count as verification evidence instead of a physical test.
nodes.status_oct2026: Not available (general): mainstream engines (MuJoCo, Drake, PhysX/Isaac) use different contact regularizations with no certified error bounds. Not addressed by the catalog.
nodes.why: Space robotics qualification leans on physical testing in low-fidelity analogs (air-bearing tables, parabolic flights, dirty thermal-vacuum chambers). A certified simulator, validated against a modest set of vacuum and dust experiments, could replace a large share of those tests with analysis. The math is cognitive-clock work under S2; the binding gate is the validation experiments for dusty, cold, vacuum contact.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Error bounds will be conditional on parameters measured in the lab; for lunar dust (electrostatic adhesion, cold welding, abrasion) parameter uncertainty dominates and certified numerics only shrink the smaller error term.
nodes.signpost: A contact solver released with a formal convergence proof (e.g. inside Drake or MuJoCo), and a NASA ISAM or Moon Base program accepting its results as verification evidence.

nodes.title: Honest reliability numbers for life support
nodes.description: System-of-systems reliability, sparing and crew-maintenance models for regenerative life support with Bayesian uncertainty from ISS failure history: the analysis that decides how many tonnes of spares a Mars crew carries and how much crew time maintenance eats.
nodes.status_oct2026: Methods exist (Langley's EMAT, semi-Markov sparing, Bayesian estimation) but scale poorly to system-of-systems; last public ECLSS reliability data release was 2004 (ICES 2025). A 2025 Bayesian study estimates 907 crew-hours of ECLSS maintenance (~45 min/day) and availability 0.9687 for a 1,200-day mission. 'Solved in principle, expert-scarce and data-limited'.
nodes.why: In the 2025 study the 5th-percentile spares mass matches a 10x MTBF improvement, i.e. the uncertainty band spans an order of magnitude in MTBF. A model that uses every ISS failure record, component physics and shelf-life data, with uncertainty propagated end to end, narrows that band; if it halves MTBF uncertainty, spares mass at fixed risk could fall ~20-40% (general estimate). Under S2 this is routine AI applied statistics by 2027, gated by NASA releasing the data.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Thin data cannot be cured by better math; failure data accrue only with operating hours, and ISS, the only large source, retires around 2030-2032 (extension to 2032 proposed). Better UQ may simply confirm the wide band.
nodes.signpost: NASA publishes an updated ISS ECLSS failure and replacement dataset; Mars architecture studies cite AI-built sparing models.

nodes.title: Fast, trustworthy models of oxygen reactors
nodes.description: Reduced-order multiphysics models (electrochemistry, melt flow and heat transfer, gas evolution, composition drift) of molten-regolith electrolysis, carbothermal and solid-oxide reactors, with error bounds, used for model-predictive control, optimal test design and scale-up decisions.
nodes.status_oct2026: Bespoke per team. LR-1 MRE: 0.07 kg O2/h for 9 h on 25 kg simulant in vacuum (ICES 2026); CaRD solar-carbothermal integrated test completed Feb 2026 (no public rate); MOXIE peak 12 g/h; OxEon MOMS designing for 1-3 kg/h O2 with >65% CO2-to-CH4 conversion and 5,000+ h stack tests. Melt composition, liquidus and viscosity drift during electrolysis (Acta Astronautica 2025).
nodes.why: Going from 0.07 kg/h to a 10 t/yr plant (~1.1 kg/h continuous at under 30 kW, 2025 systems study) is a ~16x step for MRE; MOXIE to MOMS is ~80-250x. Each build-test cycle costs months; good ROMs plus Bayesian experiment design cut the number of cycles, and MPC handles regolith composition drift. Under S2 this is routine AI applied math by 2028.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The uncertainty sits in property data at 1,600 C (melt viscosity and conductivity vs composition, anode corrosion), not in model reduction; teams already run COMSOL-class models. Plant performance is capped by hardware life and power, which models do not change.
nodes.signpost: An ISRU payload flies with model-predictive control built on a published reduced-order model; ICES or Acta Astronautica papers report AI-generated reactor ROMs validated against test data.

nodes.title: Validated models of digging icy regolith
nodes.description: Calibrated, well-posed continuum-plus-DEM models of excavation, conveying and trafficability for polar regolith, including ice-cemented and vapor-deposited ice forms, predictive enough to size excavators and water-extraction feeders.
nodes.status_oct2026: Lab-only. Ice-cemented simulant: excavation energy 2.74 to 143 J/g as ice rises 1 to 12 wt% (52x); pressure-sintered: 0.35 to 0.11 J/g (Space and Planetary Resources, Sep 2026). DEM calibration with realistic particle shapes and agglutinates ongoing (2024-2026). The ice form at the poles is unknown.
nodes.why: Without knowing the ice form, excavator power and wear sizing is uncertain by more than 10x. A well-posed model calibrated on lab simulants and then tested blind against the first in-situ polar data (2028) becomes a design basis. S3 cannot beat S2 here because the gate is the ground-truth mission, not cognition.
nodes.strongest_case_small: One or two landing sites may not represent the variability across permanently shadowed regions; designers will overbuild regardless, and early ice mining may target easier deposits.
nodes.signpost: VIPER or another polar lander returns geotechnical data, and a published model predicts it blind within a factor of two.

nodes.title: Anodes that survive molten regolith
nodes.description: Discovery and life prediction of inert anode and crucible materials for oxygen-evolving electrolysis of molten regolith at ~1,600 C, the component that limits molten-regolith-electrolysis plant life.
nodes.status_oct2026: Active research: iridium anodes (costly), zirconia-based hollow anodes (Acta Astronautica, Jun 2025). Longest reported integrated large-scale run: hours (LR-1, 9 h). Plants need thousands of hours.
nodes.why: A 10 t/yr plant with anodes lasting 1,000 h needs ~8 anode swaps a year, each a robotic maintenance operation in a 1,600 C cell; at 10,000 h it needs fewer than one. AI-guided and autonomous-lab materials search (S2/S3) can shortlist compositions quickly, but each candidate still needs a multi-thousand-hour endurance test.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Endurance testing is inherently slow (10,000 h is about 14 months per test) and AI cannot compress it; and the carbothermal route avoids the inert-anode problem entirely, so the whole node may be bypassed.
nodes.signpost: A continuous MRE run longer than 1,000 h reported; an AI-discovered anode composition published with endurance data.

nodes.title: Bioregenerative loops with stability guarantees
nodes.description: Multi-compartment models of bioregenerative life support (bacteria, algae, higher plants, crew) with certified stability and recovery margins, and controllers designed against those margins.
nodes.status_oct2026: MELiSSA pilot plant has integrated liquid streams of three compartments and prepared gas closure across four (ICES 2025); a 2025 npj Microgravity review flags critical US capability gaps in bioregenerative systems. Family 149 (T1; possible T3 per repo docs) proves permanence for closed weakly reversible mass-action networks, an idealized building block.
nodes.premise_tier: T1 (149 part is conditional); main channel is capability
nodes.why: Instability (microbial washout, crop failure, CO2/O2 imbalance) is the main operational risk of bioregenerative systems and the reason they carry large physico-chemical backups. Certified stability margins define safe operating envelopes and shrink buffer stocks. 149 contributes only the idealized guarantee that a closed mass-action core cannot lose a species; the real value is AI building validated reduced models and Lyapunov or permanence-type certificates for the controlled loop. The 149-dependent part is conditional (T1).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Biology is not mass-action and real failures come from contamination, disease and equipment; validation needs months-to-years closed tests, so the model may only re-describe what operators already manage empirically.
nodes.signpost: MELiSSA or a Chinese Lunar Palace successor publishes model-based loop control with stability certificates validated over a multi-month closed run.

nodes.title: Narrower uncertainty on crew radiation risk
nodes.description: Mechanistic radiobiology models (high-LET track structure, non-targeted effects, dose-rate) that shrink the uncertainty on cancer and cardiovascular risk per unit dose for Moon and Mars crews.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA limit: 600 mSv career effective dose, independent of age and sex. Space Weather (Mar 2026): staying under 600 mSv on a Mars mission requires flying near solar maximum or faster transfers. Tomography review (Jul 2026): recent NASA Space Cancer Risk model revisions and non-targeted-effect scenarios suggest risks may be higher than earlier estimates; uncertainty remains substantial for high-LET radiobiology. Transport models predict dose well (blind Artemis I validation, 2025).
nodes.why: Risk-per-dose uncertainty drives shielding mass and allowed mission duration. Halving it could relax design margins, but that requires new biological data: animal cohorts (years to cancer endpoints), organoid and beam studies at NSRL (limited beam time). S3's autonomous labs could scale in-vitro work, but in-vivo latency is a fixed physical clock.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The 600 mSv limit is a policy choice, not a model output, and is unlikely to move within five years whatever models say; dose physics (not math) sets the mass needed to shield.
nodes.signpost: NASA revises its Space Cancer Risk model with mechanistic components, or changes the 600 mSv standard.

nodes.title: Proof-carrying autonomy for lunar robots
nodes.description: Rover, excavator and LTV flight software whose planner, fault responses and safety monitors ship with machine-checked proofs: a synthesized planner plus a runtime-assurance wrapper around learned perception, produced by AI agents at a cost a commercial lunar company can afford.
nodes.status_oct2026: Not flown. CADRE (late 2026, IM-3) demonstrates multi-robot autonomy (leader election, task re-allocation, cooperative mapping) without proofs; Perseverance's AI-planned drives (Dec 2025) used digital-twin checking. LTV awards (May 2026: Astrolab $219M, Lunar Outpost $220M; Pegasus offers manual, autonomous and remote modes).
nodes.why: Moon Base Phase 1 (up to 30 CLPS landings from 2027) puts many robots on the surface with small operations teams; verification cost per autonomous behavior becomes the binding cost of autonomy. Agents that synthesize and prove planners and wrap learned components in proven monitors collapse that cost. Uncrewed commercial robots need no regulator, so no Medium cap applies; NASA software assurance acceptance is the qualification gate.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Most lunar robot losses so far are hardware and environment (landers tipping, thermal, dust, comms), not logic errors; proofs cover the model, not the Moon.
nodes.signpost: A CLPS, LTV or NASA payload provider advertises formally verified autonomy with published proof artifacts; NASA's Fly Foundational Robotics mission or CADRE follow-ons adopt them.

nodes.title: Crew-side fault diagnosis without Mission Control
nodes.description: Onboard diagnosis and repair guidance for habitats, life support and crew medicine that a crew 4-24 light-minutes from Earth can trust: model-based reasoning and AI assistants whose conclusions are cross-checked against verified system models.
nodes.status_oct2026: Research prototypes: DARIA/STAMPS anomaly-response architecture (AIAA SciTech, Jan 2026); NASA's progressively Earth-independent medical operations (EIMO) framework names clinical AI as a high-value target (2025); AI-assisted medical diagnostics tests on ISS reported in Mar 2026 (press headline only). ISS relies on ground engineering teams.
nodes.why: Mars crews face light-time delays and blackouts; ECLSS maintenance alone is estimated at ~45 min/day. Faster, trustworthy diagnosis cuts downtime, spares and risk. As an advisory tool (crew decides) it needs adoption, not certification; Gateway's pause (Mar 2026) moves the uncrewed-habitat testbed role to ISS and the Moon base.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Advisory AI is already available; trust, training and procedures, not mathematics, limit adoption, and for the Moon (1.3 s delay) NASA will keep the ground in the loop.
nodes.signpost: NASA flies an onboard diagnostic assistant with a formal cross-check component on ISS or an Artemis landing mission.

nodes.title: Design excavators from models, not guesses
nodes.description: Model-based sizing and design optimization of excavators, conveyors and ice-processing feeders for polar regolith, replacing much of today's build-and-dig-in-simulant iteration.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA's IPEx is designed to excavate on the order of 20 t of regolith per mission; designs are iterated in simulant test bins. 2026 work on bucket design uses vision-based fill analysis (arXiv 2609.25724).
nodes.why: With a validated regolith model, AI multiphysics design optimization can trade bucket geometry, power and wear against the in-situ ice form, avoiding a 10x over- or under-sized machine. The gate is the ground-truth data and model validation, not the optimizer.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Excavator mass is a small share of a lunar base; conservative over-design costs little compared with landing slots, so precision design may not change what flies.
nodes.signpost: An ISRU excavator or ice-mining payload selected for a 2029-2031 flight with a model-based design report validated against in-situ data.

nodes.title: Reliable recipes for sintering regolith
nodes.description: Process windows and closed-loop control for microwave, solar or laser sintering and melting of regolith into landing pads, roads and blast berms, avoiding thermal-stress cracking in lunar thermal extremes.
nodes.status_oct2026: Multiphysics modeling (Coatings, Feb 2026) finds microwave-sintered bodies crack when cooled faster than ~16 C/min (safe below 15 C/min). Startups pursuing lunar construction: Lunar Forge (Jul 2026), Astroport with Vermeer on autonomous construction machinery (Apr 2026). Plume-surface interaction models that set pad requirements are immature (see prop-psi-models).
nodes.why: Coupled electromagnetic-thermal-stress models are expert-scarce but well-posed; AI can map process windows across regolith compositions and design controllers that hold cooling rates, cutting the test matrix. Pads matter because landing plumes eject regolith at high speed, a hazard that grows with Starship-class landers.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Regolith composition and grain size vary by site; vacuum-thermal test facilities are scarce; and on the Moon the binding constraint is kW-to-100s-of-kW power for sintering, not recipes.
nodes.signpost: A relevant-environment test produces sintered pads that survive a rocket-plume test; a CLPS manifest includes a construction demo.

nodes.title: Robot assembly skills with proven safety envelopes
nodes.description: Learned or optimized manipulation skills (connector mating, truss and solar-array assembly, cable routing, refueling interfaces) wrapped in certified contact simulation and runtime assurance, so qualification can lean on analysis rather than exhaustive physical testing.
nodes.status_oct2026: Northrop Grumman's Mission Robotic Vehicle launched Jul 22, 2026 with two NRL robotic arms and three Mission Extension Pods; NASA's Fly Foundational Robotics mission (Motiv arm, PickNik MoveIt Pro on Space ROS, Feb 2026) targets autonomous and ground-supervised manipulation. Industry calls assembly the ISAM capability 'furthest from reality' (Payload, Apr 2026).
nodes.why: Contact-rich assembly is where learned policies outperform hand-coded ones, but they are hard to qualify. Certified contact simulation provides envelope evidence; runtime assurance keeps the learned policy inside it. The binding gate is validating the envelope in vacuum and microgravity analogs.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Customers buy servicing (inspection, life extension, refueling) with scripted, teleoperated arms; large-scale assembly lacks a paying customer before Starship-era structures, so the technique may wait for demand rather than math.
nodes.signpost: MRV or FFR on-orbit results reporting autonomous contact tasks under a runtime-assurance monitor; a program accepting simulation evidence for a contact task.

nodes.title: First measurements of how hard polar ice is to dig
nodes.description: In-situ geotechnical and volatile data from lunar south-pole regolith (VIPER, CLPS drills, Chang'e-7, LUPEX, Moon Base Phase 1 rovers): the physical data gate for every excavation and water-extraction model.
nodes.status_oct2026: PRIME-1 drill on IM-2 (Mar 2025) returned limited data after the lander tipped over (general). VIPER delivery tasked to Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mk1 (Dec 2025 task order), but the May 28, 2026 New Glenn static-fire explosion destroyed LC-36 ground systems (best-case pad restoration ~15 months per reporting), and NASA is evaluating Falcon Heavy. Moon Base Phase 1 targets up to 30 CLPS landings from 2027.
nodes.why: This node exists to show a gate AI cannot move: the excavation models above cannot be validated until a polar lander digs. Multiple independent attempts (US, China, India/Japan) make data by 2031 likely in every scenario; S2/S3 do not change the date.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Data from one or two sites may not generalize across permanently shadowed regions, leaving models under-constrained even after first contact.
nodes.signpost: Blue Moon Mk1 with VIPER launch date after the LC-36 rebuild; Chang'e-7 or LUPEX polar operations.

nodes.title: First oxygen made on the Moon
nodes.description: A flight demonstration that extracts measurable oxygen (grams to kilograms) from lunar regolith on the surface, by carbothermal reduction, molten-regolith electrolysis or another route.
nodes.status_oct2026: Ground prototypes only: CaRD integrated solar-carbothermal test (Feb 2026), LR-1 MRE (0.07 kg/h, late 2024), Blue Origin Air Pioneer MRE (Jun 2026). NASA's lunar ISRU strategy is a leader/follower sequence of flight demos leading to a pilot plant (NTRS 2025).
nodes.why: AI-built reactor models and test design can pull flight-unit readiness forward by about a year in S2/S3, but the date is set by CLPS manifests and lander success. Recent CLPS-era landing outcomes have been mixed (several tip-overs and failures, general), so even with many 2027-2031 flights the demo stays Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The demo would happen on roughly this schedule without AI math; oxygen chemistry from regolith was shown on the ground decades ago, and the bottleneck is a landing slot, power and dust-tolerant hardware.
nodes.signpost: An ISRU oxygen payload manifested on a named 2027-2029 CLPS mission.

nodes.title: A lunar robot flies proof-carrying autonomy
nodes.description: A rover, excavator or LTV operates on the Moon using autonomy software whose planner and safety monitors carry machine-checked proofs.
nodes.status_oct2026: None. CADRE (late 2026) will be the first autonomous multi-robot team on the Moon, without proofs.
nodes.why: Once proof-carrying autonomy is cheap (S2 2028), adoption needs only one willing payload provider and one successful landing; with up to 30 CLPS landings planned from 2027 and LTVs arriving with Artemis IV, several opportunities exist before 2031. In S3 cheap proofs arrive earlier and become a default supplier practice.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Providers may see no customer pull for proofs on uncrewed robots, and landing failures may consume the opportunities.
nodes.signpost: A lunar mission press kit or NASA payload description lists formally verified autonomy as a feature.

nodes.title: Long closed life-support test run by certified control
nodes.description: A ground test of 180+ days in which a bioregenerative or hybrid life-support loop runs under model-based control with stability certificates, at higher closure (food, O2, water) than prior tests.
nodes.status_oct2026: Precedent: China's Lunar Palace 1 ran a 370-day crewed closed test in 2017-18 (general); MELiSSA pilot plant progressing toward full loop closure with rat crew mock-up (2025).
nodes.why: Crop cycles (60-120 days, general) and the need to observe disturbances and recoveries make the test inherently months long; S3 autonomous labs can run more parallel small-scale loops, but a crew-scale test still takes calendar time.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Funding, not modeling, has limited US bioregenerative work (npj Microgravity 2025); a better controller does not create a test facility.
nodes.signpost: Announcement of a new long-duration closed-loop campaign (MELiSSA full loop, Lunar Palace successor, or a NASA/commercial analog) citing model-based stability control.

nodes.title: Robotic assembly in space with certified skills
nodes.description: An on-orbit or lunar-surface demonstration of multi-step robotic assembly (structure, array or connector mating) using learned or optimized skills qualified mainly by certified simulation plus runtime assurance.
nodes.status_oct2026: MRV (launched Jul 2026) begins servicing operations; FFR in development; OSAM-1 was cancelled in 2024 (general).
nodes.why: Needs the certified-skills toolchain (S2 2030) and a flight slot; servicing vehicles already on orbit could host a software-upgraded demo, which is why S3 reaches Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: No paying assembly customer before Starship-era structures; demonstrations remain government-funded one-offs.
nodes.signpost: MRV or a successor performing an autonomous multi-step contact task beyond grapple-and-dock.

nodes.title: Kilogram-per-hour propellant production on Mars
nodes.description: A MOMS-class solid-oxide unit (1-3 kg O2/h plus methane) operating on Mars, 80-250x MOXIE's peak rate.
nodes.status_oct2026: OxEon MOMS hardware in design (ICES 2026). SpaceX reached orbit with Starship on Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026); ship-to-ship propellant transfer is expected in early 2027; Musk called a 2026 Mars attempt a 'distraction' (Jan 2026 headline). Remaining Mars departure windows in the horizon: late 2028/early 2029 and early 2031.
nodes.why: Only two windows fit in the horizon. Operation by 2031 essentially requires a successful Starship (or other) Mars landing from the 2028-29 window carrying an ISRU unit. AI math cannot add windows, shorten transits or raise landing reliability; S3 equals S2.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Everything here is launch, landing and power; the math contribution is a slightly better-tuned reactor.
nodes.signpost: SpaceX or NASA announces a 2028 Mars cargo manifest that includes ISRU hardware.

nodes.title: AI plans rover operations, machines check the plans
nodes.description: Routine use of AI agents to plan multi-sol rover traverses and multi-robot surface activities, with automated simulation and formal checks replacing most human plan review.
nodes.status_oct2026: Demonstrated once at Mars: Perseverance's first AI-planned drives on Dec 8 and 10, 2025 (210 m and 246 m; Claude vision-language models used orbital imagery and slope data to lay waypoints), checked via JPL's digital twin across more than 500,000 telemetry variables (JPL, Jan 30, 2026). JPL describes a goal of kilometer-scale drives with minimal operator workload.
nodes.why: This is the capability channel in its purest form: no catalog theorem is involved. Ground operations dominate extended-mission cost, and the Moon Base plan multiplies the number of robots per operator. Formal plan checking (model checking of command sequences against flight rules) makes AI plans acceptable without line-by-line human review.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Already happening without any new mathematics; rover productivity is capped by power, comm passes, hazards and science-team decision time, not planning.
nodes.signpost: JPL reports a majority of a rover's drives in a quarter as AI-planned, or a kilometer-scale AI-planned drive; Moon Base robot operators adopt the same workflow.

nodes.title: Lunar base runs itself between crew visits
nodes.description: Robots, LTVs and base systems operate, maintain and resupply lunar base elements autonomously for months between crewed landings, with Earth supervising rather than commanding.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 24, 2026): phased build-up, crewed landings initially every six months, Gateway paused in its current form; budget reported at ~$30B with bulk launch buys near (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6, 2026). Artemis III is a 2027 Earth-orbit test; first landing 2028. Lunar Reactor-1 fission system to land in 2030.
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (102 T3, 124 T1 for planning ceilings only)
nodes.why: Between six-month crew visits a base has months of idle infrastructure that must be maintained (dust, thermal cycling, power management). Cognitive enablers are ready by 2028 in S2; the binding gate is that there must be enough base to operate: power (2030 reactor), habitats and logistics delivered by 2029-2031. Gateway's pause removes the planned uncrewed-habitat autonomy testbed, so the surface base inherits that role.
nodes.strongest_case_small: With a 1.3 s light-time, the Moon can be run by teleoperation and ground scheduling; autonomy is a cost saver, not an enabler, and little base infrastructure will exist by 2031.
nodes.signpost: NASA Moon Base Phase 2 contracts specifying autonomous operations between crewed missions; LTVs operating uncrewed for months after Artemis IV.

nodes.title: Tonne-per-year lunar oxygen plant
nodes.description: An operational lunar oxygen plant producing at least ~1 t/yr toward a 10 t/yr pilot scale, feeding life support and lander propellant.
nodes.status_oct2026: No flight unit. A 2025 systems study sketches 10 t/yr by molten regolith electrolysis at under 30 kW with vertical solar arrays and an excavator.
nodes.why: Needs the flight demo (2028-2030), then a funded pilot plant, tens of kW of continuous power, regolith handling and maintenance robots; the leader/follower demo sequence plus landing cadence puts operations after 2031 except under S3 with everything going right.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Every gate is physical (power, landed mass, funding, hardware life); AI math shaves design time on a path dominated by launch cadence.
nodes.signpost: NASA funds an ISRU pilot plant as part of Moon Base Phase 2 with a named delivery date.

nodes.title: Mars-class closed-loop life support, demonstrated
nodes.description: Regenerative ECLSS with at least 98% water recovery, 75%+ oxygen recovery and demonstrated reliability good enough for a ~1,000-day Mars mission, flown on ISS, a commercial station or a lunar habitat.
nodes.status_oct2026: ISS: 98% water recovery (2023); Exploration ECLSS testbed integration on ISS in progress (ICES Jul 2026); ISS extension to 2032 proposed. Oxygen recovery from CO2 on ISS is roughly half (general).
nodes.why: Reliability is demonstrated with operating hours: a zero-failure demonstration of MTBF M at 95% confidence needs about 3M unit-hours (general). For an assembly with a 20,000 h MTBF target that is ~60,000 unit-hours, about 7 unit-years, so parallel units and years of operation are required. AI can design better hardware and tests, but not compress hours; S3's autonomous labs could run many parallel ground units, hence Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The gap is hardware maturity and test time, which math does not touch; ISS retirement may end the only long-duration flight testbed before demonstration completes.
nodes.signpost: Exploration ECLSS units accumulate multi-year ISS run time with published failure data; a commercial station adopts closed-loop O2 recovery.

nodes.title: Starship-scale propellant plant on Mars
nodes.description: Mars ISRU producing on the order of 1,000 t of methane and oxygen per return flight: about 65 kg O2/h over ~500 days, roughly 5,000x MOXIE's peak rate, plus water-ice mining and order-1-MW continuous power (general estimates).
nodes.status_oct2026: No hardware at this scale; MOXIE demonstrated 12 g/h; MOMS targets 1-3 kg/h.
nodes.why: Requires landed megawatt-class power, ice mining and a sub-scale demo first, across 26-month windows. Even a perfect design in 2027 could not be landed, assembled and run at scale before 2031.
nodes.strongest_case_small: This is the case: the effect of AI mathematics on this node inside the horizon is nil.
nodes.signpost: SpaceX discloses a Mars power and ISRU architecture with flight hardware in test.

nodes.title: Ten times more robot work per operator
nodes.description: Useful surface work (km driven, kg excavated, tasks completed) per ground-operator hour rises about tenfold versus 2025 practice, through AI planning, multi-robot coordination and verified autonomy.
nodes.status_oct2026: Baseline: large ground teams plan rover activities daily (general); first AI-planned Mars drives Dec 2025; CADRE multi-robot demo late 2026.
nodes.why: Moon Base Phase 1 cannot be staffed like MER/MSL-era teams per robot; planning automation plus cheap verification removes the operator bottleneck. This is the domain's largest five-year outcome and rests on the capability, not the catalog.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Productivity is bounded by power (two-week nights), comm windows, dust and hardware failures; operator hours may not be the binding constraint for most robots.
nodes.signpost: NASA or a CLPS provider reports operator-hours per km or per tonne excavated falling severalfold across successive missions.

nodes.title: Mars outpost logistics cut by a third
nodes.description: Validated ISRU, closed-loop life support and robot-first precursors reduce Earth-supplied mass for a first Mars outpost by roughly 30-40%.
nodes.status_oct2026: Industry model (33FG, May 2025): a 10-person Mars outpost needs ~152 t of cargo; ISRU is ~40% of cargo cost, life support ~20% of mass, power ~25% of mass; a robot-only precursor cuts ~29% of cost and ~36% of mass but cannot delete ISRU, power and construction.
nodes.why: Needs Mars ISRU validated on Mars, Mars-class ECLSS validated in flight and crew-optional operations proven on the Moon, each gated by physical clocks extending to or past 2031.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Even under S3, the validation chain runs through Mars windows and reliability hours; design studies can claim the savings earlier, but validated savings arrive after 2031.
nodes.signpost: A Mars architecture study from NASA or SpaceX that books ISRU and closure savings against flight-validated data.

scenario_contrast: S1 (Plateau): research-grade math reaches outside teams around 2027-28 and diffuses slowly. The domain's expert-scarce work (reliability models, reactor ROMs, synthesized planners) becomes routine around 2029-2030; open problems (frictional contact, granular well-posedness) stay open; proof-carrying autonomy first flies around 2031. 13 of 30 nodes have an earliest year of 2031 or sooner, mostly operations planning, analysis tools and the first lunar oxygen demo. S2 (Exponential, base case): the cognitive clock collapses. Every tier 1-2 node and most tier 3-4 nodes in this domain arrive in 2027-2029, including credible attacks on contact mechanics and granular rheology. The tree then hits a physical wall: polar ground-truth data (2028), CLPS landing success, the 2030 lunar fission reactor, Mars windows (late 2028, early 2031), endurance tests for anodes, and reliability hours for life support. Results: routine AI-planned operations (2027), proof-carrying lunar autonomy (2028 tool, 2029 flight), a 10x operator-productivity gain (2029), first lunar oxygen (2029), crew-optional lunar operations (2031); tonne-scale lunar oxygen, Mars-class life support, narrower radiation risk and Mars propellant plants stay beyond 2031. 25 of 30 nodes have an earliest year of 2031 or sooner (earliest year, not likelihood: several carry Low or Medium bands). S3 (Recursive): cognitive nodes move about a year earlier, and autonomous labs compress experiment-gated nodes (anode materials, bioregenerative tests, many parallel reliability units) by about a year. Launch windows, landing reliability, surface power, biology (cancer latency, crop cycles) and endurance hours do not compress, so S3 adds only 3 nodes over S2 (narrower radiation risk, tonne-per-year lunar oxygen and Mars-class life support, all at the 2031 edge with Low-to-Medium bands; 28 of 30) and leaves the Mars propellant plant and the Mars logistics outcome beyond 2031.
key_insights: This domain's math is overwhelmingly bespoke and 'solved in principle but expert-scarce' (autonomy verification, reliability and sparing, reactor models, mission planning). On-demand research math matters far more here than any catalog theorem; only 104, 149 and the hardness family (102, 124, 125, 110, 111) touch the domain, all through ceilings (P3) or model confidence (P5).

The capability channel has already reached flight operations: Perseverance's AI-planned drives (Dec 2025) show the first-order effect is cognitive and near-term. What AI math adds is the second step, machine-checked plans and proof-carrying autonomy, which makes AI planning acceptable without line-by-line human review (S2: tool 2028, first lunar flight 2029).

Two genuinely open problems with real engineering leverage are not in the catalog: well-posedness and convergence for frictional multi-contact dynamics (the sim-to-real gap for grasping, docking and assembly) and well-posed continuum models for dense granular flow (excavation and construction). Negative answers would be as useful as positive ones, because they mark where simulation results are artifacts.

ISRU is a hardware, power and test problem with a vast scale gap: 0.07 kg O2/h (MRE, 2024) and 12 g/h (MOXIE) versus ~1.1 kg/h for a 10 t/yr lunar plant and ~65 kg O2/h for a Starship return. AI compresses design iterations by perhaps a year; it cannot compress anode endurance tests (10^4 h), test-facility throughput, surface power (fission arrives 2030) or Mars windows.

The data gate binds the regolith chain: excavation energy varies 52x across plausible polar ice forms. No model, however well-posed, can be validated before a polar lander digs (about 2028 in every scenario, with VIPER exposed to the New Glenn pad loss).

Life-support reliability is demonstrated in operating hours: a zero-failure 95%-confidence demonstration needs about 3x the target MTBF in unit-hours. Better math narrows the order-of-magnitude MTBF uncertainty in today's sparing estimates, but ISS (the only long-duration testbed, retiring around 2030-2032) sets the clock.
Radiation and biology are near-nil effects: dose transport is already accurate, the 600 mSv limit is policy, and risk-per-dose uncertainty needs in-vivo data on multi-year cycles.

The strategic five-year outcome is operational, not physical: roughly tenfold more robot work per operator and, under S2, crew-optional lunar base operations by about 2031. NASA's pivot from Gateway to a surface Moon Base (Mar 2026; 30 CLPS landings from 2027) is the demand signal that makes this the place AI math shows up first.
nil_effects: Mars launch windows (late 2028/early 2029, early 2031) and transit times: orbital mechanics, not mathematics, limit Mars ISRU and outpost chains to at most two attempts in the horizon.
Starship-scale Mars propellant production before 2032: needs landed megawatt-class power, ice mining and a sub-scale demo first; Speculative in every scenario.
Deep-space radiation dose rate and the mass needed to shield against it: physics fixes these; the 600 mSv career limit is policy and unlikely to move by 2031.
Biological clocks: crop growth cycles (60-120 days), animal-model cancer latency (years) and crew physiology studies cannot be accelerated by AI mathematics.
Lunar night (~14 Earth days), polar thermal extremes and abrasive, electrostatically clinging dust: environmental constraints on surface robots that set duty cycles regardless of autonomy quality.
Endurance and reliability evidence: anode life tests (10^3-10^4 h) and ECLSS MTBF demonstrations (about 3x MTBF in unit-hours at 95% confidence) run on calendar time.
Lander success rates and lift capacity (e.g. the May 2026 New Glenn pad loss delaying Blue Moon Mk1 and VIPER): physical and industrial gates on every surface demo.

Galactic speedups (107 matrix multiplication omega <= 9/4, 130 FFT below n log n) give no onboard-compute or autonomy speedup; 139 (log-concave sampling with d^epsilon queries, T3) and 140 (memory-sample lower bounds, T3) are theoretical ceilings for onboard estimation and learning with no practical change, since real posteriors are rarely well-conditioned log-concave and flight processors are not at those asymptotic limits.

signposts.event: Any lab makes research-grade math capability publicly purchasable (API or product) by mid-2027.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms the S2 timing for cap-research-math-public, pulling the synthesis, reliability-UQ and contact-mechanics nodes into 2027-2028; if access slips past 2028, shift those nodes toward S1.

signposts.event: Independent Comparator runs on openai/math families 104 (RandomizedMeanPayoff.lean), 149 (MassAction.lean) and 124 (ThreeMachine.lean).
signposts.what_it_changes: Moves those premises to T4 and removes the 'conditional' label from the planning-ceilings and bioregenerative nodes; also resolves whether 149 and 124 are T1 (per the overview) or T3 (per lean/docs).

signposts.event: CADRE operates on the Moon after IM-3 (late 2026 or 2027) and reports leader election and task re-allocation results.
signposts.what_it_changes: Establishes the multi-robot autonomy baseline that proof-carrying autonomy improves on; a failure for software reasons would raise the value of verified autonomy.

signposts.event: JPL reports routine or kilometer-scale AI-planned drives, or a Moon Base robot operator adopts AI planning with formal plan checking.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms auton-ai-planned-ops-routine (2027) and the surface-productivity outcome; absence by end-2027 pushes both a year later.

signposts.event: A CLPS, LTV or NASA FFR provider publishes formally synthesized or proof-carrying autonomy artifacts.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms the P2 bridge for uncrewed surface robots on the S2 schedule (tool 2028, flight 2029).

signposts.event: Blue Moon Mk1/VIPER launch date after the LC-36 rebuild, and Chang'e-7 or other polar landers returning geotechnical data.
signposts.what_it_changes: Sets the date of the icy-regolith ground-truth node, which gates the whole excavation chain in every scenario.

signposts.event: An ISRU oxygen payload is manifested on a named 2027-2029 CLPS flight; an MRE or carbothermal run passes 1,000 h.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms or delays first oxygen on the Moon (S2 2029) and the anode-life node; no manifest by end-2027 pushes the demo past 2030.

signposts.event: NASA releases updated ISS ECLSS failure data, or Exploration ECLSS units report multi-year ISS run time.
signposts.what_it_changes: Unlocks the data gate for the reliability-UQ node and starts the operating-hours clock for Mars-class life support.

signposts.event: AI-produced results on frictional contact well-posedness or granular rheology appear in mechanics or applied-math venues.
signposts.what_it_changes: Confirms that the capability reaches applied PDE and nonsmooth mechanics (S2); absence through 2028 suggests the plateau scenario for applied math.

signposts.event: Starship ship-to-ship propellant transfer (expected early 2027) and any SpaceX 2028 Mars cargo manifest that includes ISRU hardware.
signposts.what_it_changes: Determines whether the Mars ISRU demo node is reachable in the 2028-29 window at all; without a manifest by 2028 it moves beyond 2031 in every scenario.
